To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) spontaneous speech can be exploited to detect Alzheimer's and mild cognitive impairment; 2) acoustic and linguistic features extracted from speech can be used to differentiate between the patient and control groups; and 3) the combination of acoustic and linguistic features is more effective than either of the two feature types individually.

(i) the acoustic and linguistic features extracted from spontaneous speech are able to differentiate between healthy controls, patients with Alzheimer's disease (mild AD) and those with mild cognitive impairments (mCI); (ii) the accuracy of the automatic classification task is comparable with the accuracy of the clinical diagnosis, and the classification results of our method are consistent with the clinical findings; and (iii) our method can serve for the automatic screening of patients with mild cognitive impairment and AD.
the automatic extraction and analysis of acoustic and linguistic features extracted from spontaneous speech can be utilized for the early diagnosis of AD and MCI.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new automatic speech processing method for the detection of mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease.
the early diagnosis of AD and MCI, and we believe our method has the potential to become part of the diagnostic procedure of these diseases.
the automatic identification of mild cognitive impairment and mild Alzheimer's based on spontaneous speech.

our results show that the spontaneous speech can be a good source for the automatic detection of Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment.

the acoustic features are more effective in separating the healthy control group from the Alzheimer's patients, while the linguistic features are more effective when separating the Alzheimer's patients from the mild cognitive impairment patients.
the proposed approach can serve as a screening tool to identify the patients with AD and MCI.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are capable of detecting the early stages of Alzheimer's disease based only on the spontaneous speech produced during a short, everyday conversation.
we are capable of identifying mild cognitive impairment and mild Alzheimer's from spontaneous speech using automatic speech recognition and linguistic features.
we have developed a method for the automatic identification of mild cognitive impairment and mild Alzheimer's patients based on the analysis of their spontaneous speech.

the automatic speech recognition based extraction of acoustic features is an effective way to identify patients with Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment.
the automatic analysis of speech can be a useful tool in the diagnosis of mild neurodegenerative diseases.
